title: Ad-libbing versus playing the melody
summary: Hall says black players improvised on melodies that white players expected to hear straight.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: It was sad to grow up into that, in an attitude where which side they went on. By this time, you couldn't

get a player that could play the verse of "Stardust." You know, this was too square for them, and in my coming up and we used to play for the gansters and all that sort of thing, crowd— We played all the songs that were composed then, standards as they are now, and then in later years when I came to New York, I find out that the white musicians figured that the black musicians didn't know the melody because they always ad-libbed.

Instead of playing the straight line, which created the date field, as is known as of now. It's all we ever used to do, you know, because we didn't know any better maybe, but this is what, you know, a song came out and you played the melody to it.
This is what got you gigs.

Yeah, yeah, but we didn't have that much, that many gigs, we didn't have that many gigs. Now, it's a corporate thing you know; it was a big deal, you know. In my day The Meyer Davis it was Lester Lanin sort of stuff. Now, all you have to do is play the melody. Anybody that has learned his instrument can play the melody and so the deviation became what is known as jazz, from the melody. Symphony players couldn't deviate. They were too disciplined to play what they had practiced all their lives.
I don't want to be putting down anybody
